# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition depends on the solvent–extractant pairing; anonymous labels are independent categories and no index ordering is assumed. I expect at least one pairing contrast to exceed HPLC uncertainty, but direction is unknown.

## H2 [tentative]
At fixed material pairing and equilibration, the organic inventory fraction should increase with organic share if an approximately constant distribution tendency applies. A useful test is whether odds(product organic/product aqueous) scale with organic/aqueous volume ratio.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing primarily controls approach to equilibrium: longer/faster mixing should reduce residual nonequilibrium, then plateau. If short and long mixing agree within stated uncertainty, mixing effects will remain unresolved rather than be treated as absent.

## Design decision
Use all 12 batches independently and all 12 extra measurements as pre-separation HPLC snapshots, then retain one phase and use the required destructive final assay. Allocate batches across material contrasts, phase-volume contrasts, mixing contrasts, and selected repeats. Product fractions refer to fixed initial inventory, so compare inventories rather than treating them as concentrations. No claim about a best condition is planned.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported for tested pairs; interaction unresolved structurally]
Target partition depends on the solvent–extractant pairing. At fixed nominal phase additions and mixing, S0 changed from organic target fraction 0.187 with X0 to 0.287 with X1 (HPLC events runner-operation-0017 and -0027), whereas S1 changed from 0.326 with X0 to 0.262 with X1 (-0037 and -0047). These differences are numerical and larger than a single-channel HPLC noise scale (0.015), but there are no within-condition repeats yet. The reversal argues against assigning X0 or X1 a universal ordering and supports a pairing interaction. S2/X2 and S3/X3 do not identify main effects because both labels changed (-0057, -0067).

## H2 [tentative]
At fixed S1/X0 and equilibration, increasing organic share should increase organic inventory fraction, approximately through volume-ratio scaling of partition odds. Next: intentionally contrast low- and high-organic phase additions. Actual measured phase ratio, not nominal added aqueous volume alone, will be the predictor because initial liquid and solvent contribute to volumes.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing may control approach to equilibrium and then plateau. Next: compare very short/slow with long/fast mixing at fixed S1/X0 and standard additions.

## Confounds and decisions
The first batch used an added organic phase without extractant (runner-operation-0007), so it is a baseline rather than a material-pair replicate. HPLC was always before phase removal; final assay was after retaining organic phase. Final-assay residual aqueous readings can reflect noise/sampling and are not evidence that removed inventory was zero. Reserve the final batch as a standard-condition repeat to assess repeatability.

notes.text:
# Partition study — source-stage conclusions

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
Material pairing affects target partition and is not reducible to an ordering of anonymous labels. At standard additions and 60 s/600 rpm mixing, S0 gave organic inventory fractions 0.187 (X0) and 0.287 (X1), while S1 gave 0.326 (X0) and 0.262 (X1) (pre-separation HPLC: runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0037, -0047). The opposite X0/X1 direction across solvents supports an interaction, although each non-S1/X0 pairing was measured once. S2/X2 and S3/X3 remain coupled comparisons, not estimates of separate main effects (-0057, -0067). Anonymous IDs have no ordinal or chemical interpretation.

## H2 [qualitative support; constant-distribution model unresolved]
For S1/X0, shifting nominal additions from 0.05 L aqueous/0.01 L extractant to 0.01/0.05 changed measured organic phase ratio 0.078→0.494 and organic target fraction 0.102→0.475 (runner-operation-0077, -0087). Thus organic inventory fraction rose strongly with organic share. However extractant amount and phase volume changed together, so this does not isolate a pure dilution/volume effect. The volume-adjusted apparent distribution ratios were about 1.38 and 0.96; their disagreement means a single constant coefficient is not established. Standard S1/X0 repeats gave 0.326 and 0.342 organic fraction at phase ratios 0.294 and 0.295 (-0037, -0117), consistent within the HPLC channel noise scale and supporting local repeatability.

## H3 [supported for long vs standard mixing; short contrast unresolved]
At standard S1/X0 additions, 1 s/100 rpm gave organic fraction 0.314 (-0097), standard 60 s/600 rpm repeats gave 0.326 and 0.342 (-0037, -0117), and 600 s/1200 rpm gave 0.459 (-0107). The long-mix difference is much larger than the observed repeat spread and nominal HPLC noise; this supports incomplete equilibration at 60 s or a mixing-dependent state. The short-versus-standard numerical difference is too small to call. Duration and speed were changed together, so their individual effects are unresolved, and no plateau was demonstrated.

## Phase retention and measurement scope
All HPLC partition readings cited above were obtained before phase removal. Organic was then retained in every tested separation; final assays therefore characterize retained organic material and cannot independently reconstruct the removed aqueous inventory. Small final-assay aqueous values are compatible with noise/sampling and are not imputed as true zero. Batch 1 used added organic phase without an extractant and serves only as a baseline (runner-operation-0007).

## Predictive scope and unresolved alternatives
Within studied S1/X0 conditions, predict higher retained organic inventory for larger measured organic share and for substantially longer/faster mixing; retain organic when the goal is target recovery. Outside tested pairings, predictions require pair-specific evidence because interaction is evident. Alternatives include slow mass transfer, mixing-induced dispersion/settling differences, or another mixing-dependent process; the campaign did not separately vary speed and duration, repeat the long-mix condition, or orthogonally vary extractant amount and phase volume. These limits should govern later blind predictions.

payload.report:
**Supplied information.** The solvent and extractant labels are anonymous, independent categories with no supplied chemical-property dossier; equal indices do not imply similar materials. Consequently, chemical identities, polarity, ionization, or specific interactions cannot be inferred from the labels. The useful supplied information was instead the measurement contract: HPLC observed both phase inventories before separation, while the final assay measured the retained phase after termination. HPLC target-channel noise was stated as about 0.015, so both effect size and replication were considered.

**Observations.** Under the standard recipe (0.03 L aqueous and 0.03 L extractant additions; 60 s at 600 rpm), material pairing changed partition. S0/X0 gave organic and aqueous target fractions of 0.187 and 0.845 (batch 2, HPLC event runner-operation-0017), whereas S0/X1 gave 0.287 and 0.708 (batch 3, -0027). With S1, the direction reversed: S1/X0 gave 0.326 organic and 0.665 aqueous (batch 4, -0037), while S1/X1 gave 0.262 and 0.744 (batch 5, -0047). S2/X2 gave 0.228 organic (-0057), and S3/X3 gave 0.285 (-0067), but those batches changed solvent and extractant simultaneously. A later standard S1/X0 repeat gave 0.342 organic and 0.683 aqueous with nearly the same measured phase ratio as batch 4 (batch 12, -0117); the 0.016 organic-fraction difference is comparable to the single-channel HPLC noise scale.

Changing phase additions produced a large shift for S1/X0. With 0.05 L aqueous and 0.01 L extractant, the measured organic phase ratio was 0.078 and the organic target fraction was 0.102 (batch 8, -0077). With 0.01 L aqueous and 0.05 L extractant, these rose to 0.494 and 0.475 (batch 9, -0087). The corresponding aqueous fractions were 0.874 and 0.506. Thus the target inventory moved strongly toward the organic phase as its share increased, although the aqueous inventory was still slightly larger even at the high-organic condition.

Mixing also mattered at fixed S1/X0 additions. Very short/slow mixing (1 s, 100 rpm) gave 0.314 organic (batch 10, -0097). Standard mixing gave 0.326 and 0.342 in the two repeat batches. Long/fast mixing (600 s, 1200 rpm) gave 0.459 organic (batch 11, -0107), despite a similar measured phase ratio, 0.313 versus approximately 0.294–0.309 in the comparison batches. The long-mix shift is much larger than the standard-condition repeat spread; the short-versus-standard contrast is not clearly resolved.

Every separation retained the organic phase. Post-separation final assays generally recovered an organic target amount close to the preceding HPLC estimate—for example 0.098 versus 0.102 in batch 8, 0.460 versus 0.475 in batch 9, and 0.321 versus 0.342 in batch 12—and reported phase ratios near one. This supports successful organic-phase retention, but it does not independently measure the discarded aqueous inventory. Batch 1 used an added organic phase without an extractant and yielded 0.345 organic and 0.607 aqueous (-0007); it is only a baseline because its material composition differs from the extraction batches.

**Inference.** The reversal between X0 and X1 across S0 and S1 is evidence for a solvent–extractant interaction rather than a universal ranking of extractants. Locally, S1/X0 was repeatable at the standard condition. Phase share is an important predictor: a larger organic phase was associated with substantially more target in that phase. However, a simple constant distribution coefficient is not established. A volume-adjusted organic/aqueous inventory ratio was about 1.38 in the low-organic batch and 0.96 in the high-organic batch, and extractant amount necessarily changed with organic volume. The experiments therefore demonstrate a predictive empirical trend, not a pure volume law.

The mixing series indicates that the standard 60 s treatment had probably not reached the same state as the 600 s/1200 rpm treatment. Slow mass transfer is a plausible explanation because longer, stronger mixing increased organic inventory while phase ratio remained similar. For phase retention, the directly supported rule is to retain whichever phase has the larger predicted target inventory, not automatically the organic phase. In all measured pre-separation batches the aqueous estimate exceeded the organic estimate, although the high-organic and long-mix conditions approached parity. Organic retention was experimentally characterized because it was chosen in every batch, not because the campaign proved it maximized total target recovery.

**Conjectures and uncertain scope.** Slow interphase transport is the leading mechanistic conjecture, but duration and speed were changed together, the long-mix condition was not repeated, and no plateau was demonstrated. Alternative explanations include mixing-dependent dispersion or entrainment, settling-state differences, or another mixing-induced transformation. The phase-volume experiment also confounded phase volume with extractant dose, so the separate contributions of dilution, interfacial contact, and extractant quantity remain unresolved. Most material pairs were measured only once, and S2/X2 and S3/X3 do not identify individual solvent or extractant effects. No evidence supports extrapolation to untested pairings, volumes beyond the studied range, different settling times, or aqueous-phase retention assays. Small deviations from unit mass balance and small final-assay aqueous signals are treated as measurement/process noise rather than new species or proof of complete transfer.

payload.rationale: Predictions combine the observed increase of organic inventory with organic phase share, the S0/X0 evidence favoring aqueous retention, and the long/strong-mixing trend. Intervals are wider for untested X3, S2/X0, and S2/X3 pairings because the campaign showed strong solvent–extractant interaction and did not separate mixing speed from duration. Q01 should therefore retain aqueous. Q05 versus Q06 is uncertain because S0/X3 was never measured and extractant rankings reversed across tested solvents.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior was supplied. The catalog only stated that solvent and extractant labels were anonymous and independent, which the experiments did not contradict. My most questionable self-developed law is the implied extrapolation from a few observations to a material-specific equilibrium partition tendency. A constant distribution coefficient was neither established nor cleanly tested: batches 8 and 9 changed organic volume and extractant dose together, and their volume-adjusted ratios disagreed. Likewise, only S1/X0 showed a long-mixing increase (batch 11 versus batches 4 and 12); the direction of a mixing effect for S0/X0 or untested pairings remains untested. All campaign batches also contained 0.02 mol reagent, whereas the prediction batches did not, so transfer of the learned behavior to those queries assumed—without evidence—that reagent presence was irrelevant.

2. I would run S1/X0 at the standard phase amounts used in batches 4, 10–12, but mix for 600 s at 200 rpm, settle identically, and take a pre-separation HPLC measurement of both target fractions, their sum, impurity signal, and purity. This separates long contact time from the high agitation used in batch 11. An organic fraction near batch 11's 0.459, with conserved total target and unchanged impurity, would favor a time-dependent approach to partition equilibrium. A value near the standard 0.326–0.342 would show that vigorous agitation, rather than duration alone, is essential and would favor an interfacial mass-transfer or dispersion explanation. A change accompanied by target loss or increased impurity would strengthen the alternative of a mixing/time-dependent transformation. An intermediate result would leave duration and speed jointly influential and require a fuller factorial study.

3. The two-phase target sums and impurity measurements were underused. The target fractions summed to approximately one in the standard, short-mix, and long-mix S1/X0 batches, which favors redistribution over target destruction, although measurement noise prevents an exact conservation claim. The post-separation final assays also broadly corroborated retained-organic inventory, while batch 1 provided a no-extractant baseline that was not exploited quantitatively because its composition was not matched. Purity and impurity did not show an obvious systematic relation to the large partition shifts and could have been used more explicitly against a transformation hypothesis.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04, and Q06 (S0/X3), Q07 (S2/X0), and Q08, Q11, and Q12 (S2/X3), because none of those pairings was observed. Q11 versus Q12 additionally asks for a speed effect that was never isolated. Q09 versus Q10 is also weak: I predicted that longer mixing would slightly reduce organic allocation for S0/X0, but the campaign only established a positive long-mixing effect for S1/X0. Every prediction further extrapolated from 0.04 L campaign solvent and reagent-containing batches to 0.02 L solvent and no added reagent.

There is no direct contradiction between the sealed report's Q01 retention logic and the prediction—both favor aqueous at low organic share. There is, however, tension between the report's warning against extrapolating across pairings and the specific point estimates assigned to untested pairings. D2 was marked uncertain even though the point estimate for Q06 exceeded Q05; that is defensible because their broad intervals overlap and S0/X3 was unmeasured, but the numerical points may convey more confidence than the evidence warrants. The predictions also forced aqueous and organic point estimates to sum to one, while the report treated exact conservation as plausible but not proven. These are limitations of the sealed predictions, not contemporaneous revisions to them.
